breakfast.name: Injo Gogi Bap (Rice with Meat)
instructions: Cook rice
Season and cook ground pork
Fry egg
Serve rice topped with pork, egg, and kimchi
breakfast.description: Rice with seasoned meat, egg, and kimchi.

breakfast.name: Juk (Rice Porridge)
instructions: Cook rice in extra water until porridge
Season with sesame oil and salt
Garnish with green onion

breakfast.name: Injeolmi (Pounded Rice Cake)
ingredients: Soybean powder (roasted and slightly salted — for dusting)
instructions: Injeolmi is a traditional Korean rice cake — shared between North and South Korea
Made by steaming glutinous rice then pounding it vigorously until stretchy
The pounding is the technique — it develops the gluten of the glutinous rice into a stretchy, chewy mass
Traditional pounding used a large wooden mallet and stone block
The mochi-like texture is the result of pounding — no pounding means no texture
Roll the pounded rice in roasted soybean powder (bean powder coating)
Cut into bite-sized pieces
The soybean powder coating prevents sticking and adds nutty flavor
Injeolmi is made for celebrations, ancestral rites, and New Year (Seollal)
In North Korea, rice cakes (tteok) are central to ancestral rite tables
The making of rice cakes together is a community activity
breakfast.description: A traditional rice cake shared across the Korean peninsula — glutinous rice steamed and pounded until it forms a stretchy, mochi-like mass, then rolled in roasted soybean powder and cut into pieces. The pounding is the technique: without it, the texture cannot develop. In North Korea as in South Korea, rice cakes are central to ancestral rites and New Year celebrations.

breakfast.name: Bogeum Bap (Fried Rice, North Korean Style)
instructions: North Korean fried rice reflects the country's agricultural constraints
Vegetables are more prevalent than meat — whatever is available seasonally
Day-old rice is essential — it fries without clumping
Scramble egg in a hot, oiled pan — push to the side
Add garlic, then vegetables
Add rice, stir-fry vigorously
Season with soy sauce and salt
Finish with sesame oil — the aromatic finishing oil of Korean cuisine
North Korean cuisine relies more on local and seasonal ingredients than South Korean
Soy sauce, sesame oil, and garlic are available throughout the country
The simplicity reflects North Korean everyday cooking — resourceful with available ingredients
breakfast.description: North Korean everyday fried rice — day-old rice stir-fried with seasonal vegetables, egg, and garlic, finished with sesame oil and soy sauce. North Korean daily cooking is characterized by resourcefulness with available seasonal ingredients, with vegetables more prominent than in South Korean cooking. The sesame oil finishing is shared Korean culinary heritage across the divided peninsula.

lunch.name: Naengmyeon (Cold Buckwheat Noodles)
instructions: Make and chill beef broth
Cook buckwheat noodles, rinse in ice water
Place noodles in bowl
Add icy broth
Top with pear, cucumber, egg, kimchi
Add vinegar and mustard to taste
lunch.description: Pyongyang's signature — icy buckwheat noodles in cold beef broth.

lunch.name: Mandu (Dumplings)
ingredients: Filling: pork, tofu, kimchi, bean sprouts, green onion, sesame oil
instructions: Make dough, roll wrappers
Mix filling
Fill and pleat dumplings
Steam or boil until cooked
lunch.description: Korean dumplings with pork and kimchi.

lunch.name: Naengmyeon (Cold Buckwheat Noodles)
ingredients: Buckwheat noodles (very thin — the grey-brown buckwheat color)
Cold beef broth (chilled overnight until set — or cucumber/radish broth)
Korean radish (dongchimi — water kimchi brine also works as the broth)
Vinegar, mustard (gochujang if available — or just mustard)
instructions: Naengmyeon is Pyongyang's most famous dish — now also very popular in South Korea
Pyongyang naengmyeon is different from Hamhung naengmyeon — important distinction
Pyongyang naengmyeon: in a cold, clear beef or radish broth — mild, refreshing
Hamhung naengmyeon: dry, with a spicy sauce — hoe naengmyeon or bibim naengmyeon
Make very cold beef broth (must be chilled to near-frozen)
Cook and rinse buckwheat noodles in cold water — they should be cold and bouncy
Place in a deep bowl with ice or in icy broth
Add toppings: cucumber, pear, hard-boiled egg, sliced beef
Add vinegar and mustard for the tableside seasoning
The cold broth with slightly chewy, earthy buckwheat noodles is the experience
The Pyongyang naengmyeon restaurants in Seoul use recipes from North Korean defectors
lunch.description: North Korea's most internationally famous dish — very cold, clear beef-radish broth with thin grey-brown buckwheat noodles, garnished with pear, cucumber, egg, and sliced beef, seasoned tableside with vinegar and mustard. Pyongyang naengmyeon (mild clear broth) is distinct from Hamhung naengmyeon (spicy sauce). The Pyongyang naengmyeon restaurants in Seoul are run by North Korean defectors — the recipe crossed the border with them.

lunch.name: Janchi Guksu (Noodle Soup for Celebrations)
instructions: Janchi guksu = 'feast noodles' — noodles are the celebration food of Korea
Eating noodles at weddings means longevity and long life (the long noodles symbolize long years)
Make a clean, clear anchovy-kelp broth
The broth should be lightly seasoned — the soup is delicate
Cook noodles, rinse in cold water, place in bowls
Pour hot broth over
Top with the colorful garnishes: yellow egg strips, green zucchini, orange carrot, black seaweed
The visual arrangement matters — the colors are intentional
In North Korea, wheat noodles are available and widely eaten
Janchi guksu appears at birthdays, weddings, and sixtieth birthday parties (hwangap)
The long noodle = long life symbolism is universal across Korean culture
lunch.description: North Korea's celebration noodle soup — thin wheat noodles in a clean anchovy-kelp broth, topped with artfully arranged colorful garnishes (yellow egg, green zucchini, orange carrot, black seaweed). Eating long noodles at celebrations symbolizes long life. Janchi guksu appears at weddings, birthdays, and hwangap (60th birthday — the traditional milestone). The visual color arrangement is deliberately beautiful.

dinner.name: Kimchi Jjigae (Kimchi Stew)
instructions: Sauté pork belly
Add kimchi, stir-fry
Add water, bring to boil
Add tofu, simmer 15 min
Garnish with green onion

dinner.name: Bindaetteok (Mung Bean Pancakes)
instructions: Grind soaked beans coarsely
Mix with chopped kimchi, pork, vegetables
Fry large pancakes in oil until crispy
dinner.description: Crispy mung bean pancakes with kimchi and pork.

dinner.name: Sinsollo (Royal Hot Pot)
ingredients: Vegetables: spinach, chrysanthemum leaves, carrots, radish
instructions: Sinsollo is the royal court dish of Joseon Dynasty Korea — shared heritage
It requires a special brazier vessel with a chimney (the sinsollo vessel)
The heat rises through the chimney — the broth stays at a gentle simmer around the chimney
Prepare all ingredients carefully: meats are coated in egg and briefly fried
Vegetables are blanched separately
Arrange in the sinsollo vessel in a circular pattern — the visual arrangement is important
Pour hot beef broth over
The combination of ingredients simmering in rich broth develops into the final flavor
Sinsollo represents Korean royal court cooking — Korea's most refined culinary tradition
The sinsollo vessel is a specific Korean cooking implement — the cone-shaped chimney is the defining feature
Now made for celebrations in Korean homes with an adapted pot
dinner.description: Korean royal court hot pot — a Joseon Dynasty ceremonial dish using the sinsollo vessel (a brazier with a central chimney through which heat rises). Meats, vegetables, mushrooms, and tofu are arranged in a circular pattern around the chimney and simmered in rich beef broth. Sinsollo represents Korea's most refined culinary tradition, shared across the divided peninsula. The arrangement is as important as the flavors.

dinner.name: Kimchi Jjigae (North Korean Style)
ingredients: Fully fermented kimchi (very sour — the older the kimchi, the better for jjigae)
Gochugaru (Korean red pepper flakes) — if available in North Korea
instructions: Kimchi jjigae (kimchi stew) is one of the most fundamental Korean dishes
Made across the entire Korean peninsula — North and South
The key principle: OLD kimchi makes the best jjigae — the sourness is the point
Kimchi that is too sour to eat raw is perfect for cooking
Fry pork belly briefly in the pot
Add kimchi — fry with the pork, the fat coats the kimchi
Add water to cover
Simmer 20 minutes — the kimchi softens, the flavors merge
The resulting broth is a combination of fermented kimchi sourness and pork richness
Add tofu in the last 5 minutes (if using)
Season with soy sauce, green onion, sesame oil finishing
In North Korea, kimchi is also a staple — cabbage kimchi made with local ingredients
dinner.description: Korea's universal fermented stew — old, very sour kimchi (the more fermented the better) simmered with pork belly into a deeply savory, tangy stew. Kimchi jjigae is made across the entire Korean peninsula; North Korea's version reflects local ingredient availability. The principle is identical: sour kimchi + pork + time = one of Korea's most comforting and fundamental dishes.

snacks.name: Hotteok (Sweet Pancakes)
instructions: Make dough, rise
Fill with sugar-nut mixture
Flatten and fry until golden

imageCredit.author: Korea.net / Korean Culture and Information Service

snacks.name: Dduk (North Korean Rice Cake)
ingredients: Glutinous rice flour (or regular rice flour for certain types)
Optional: azuki bean paste, sesame seeds
instructions: Dduk (tteok) = rice cakes — one of the most ancient Korean foods
Korea has hundreds of different dduk varieties — North Korea maintains many traditional forms
Basic dduk: glutinous rice flour steamed or pounded
Mugwort (ssuk) added for the green variety — a distinctly Korean green rice cake
The flavor of ssuk: slightly bitter, herbal, aromatic — mugwort is a beloved Korean flavor
Shape: discs, logs, or stuffed with bean paste
Steam 20 minutes until cooked through
Rice cakes in North Korea: made for ancestral rites, celebrations, seasonal observances
The spring wildflower (mugwort) dduk is the most beloved traditional variety
Dduk is the fundamental Korean celebration food — appearing at every major life event
snacks.description: North Korea's traditional rice cake — steamed glutinous rice flour, often with mugwort (ssuk) for the green variety and its slightly bitter, herbal flavor. Dduk (tteok) is the most ancient Korean celebration food, appearing at every major life event from birth through death. North Korea maintains many traditional dduk forms that have been modified or commercialized in South Korea.

snacks.name: Kkakdugi (Cubed Radish Kimchi)
ingredients: Korean radish (daikon type, but Korean varieties are preferred)
Fish sauce or salted shrimp (jeotgal) — or omit for vegetarian
instructions: Kkakdugi is radish kimchi — cubed daikon in the same spiced fermented style as cabbage kimchi
Korean radish (joseon radish) is slightly sweeter and less sharp than Japanese daikon
Cube the radish into 2cm pieces — the cube shape holds its crunch through fermentation
Salt the radish pieces, let sit 30 minutes
Rinse and drain the water-released
Mix gochugaru, garlic, ginger, fish sauce, sugar — the kimchi paste
Toss radish in the paste
Ferment 1-2 days at room temperature, then refrigerate
Kkakdugi is crunchy, spicy, garlicky, slightly sweet — a different kimchi experience from cabbage
It is fermented separately but often served alongside cabbage kimchi
North Korea grows radishes abundantly — this is a year-round kimchi
snacks.description: North Korea's cubed radish kimchi — joseon radish (slightly sweeter than Japanese daikon) cut into cubes, salted and squeezed, then fermented in the gochugaru-garlic-ginger paste. The cube shape retains crunch through fermentation. Kkakdugi is a different experience from cabbage kimchi: lighter, more vegetable-forward, very crunchy. Radishes are abundant throughout Korea and this is a year-round kimchi.

snacks.name: Nokdu Jeon (Mung Bean Pancake)
ingredients: Mung beans (soaked overnight, hulled — or split yellow mung beans)
Dipping sauce: soy sauce + vinegar + chili
instructions: Nokdu jeon (bindaetteok) is a beloved Korean savory pancake — shared heritage
Mung beans soaked overnight, then blended coarsely — NOT smooth
The texture should be slightly chunky — small bean pieces in the batter
Mix with bean sprouts, green onion, garlic, ginger, salt
The batter is thick — spread and pat into pancakes on the griddle
Fry in generous oil over medium heat — the pancake needs oil to crisp
Both sides golden and crispy — the edges should be very crispy
The interior: soft, creamy from the mung bean
Dip in soy-vinegar-chili sauce
Nokdu jeon is a traditional festive Korean food — made for ancestral rites
The mung bean has been cultivated in Korea for millennia
snacks.description: Korea's traditional mung bean pancake — soaked mung beans ground coarsely (not smooth) and mixed with bean sprouts, green onion, and ginger, fried in generous oil until the edges are very crispy and the interior stays creamy. The coarse grind is essential for the right texture. Made for ancestral rites across Korea. Dipped in soy-vinegar sauce. One of Korea's oldest savory pancake traditions.

desserts.name: Songpyeon (Rice Cakes)
instructions: Make rice dough
Fill with sesame-honey mixture
Shape into half-moons
Steam on pine needles 20 min
desserts.description: Half-moon rice cakes steamed on pine needles.

desserts.name: Sikhye (Fermented Sweet Rice Drink)
ingredients: Malt barley (yeot girum — ground malt barley with active enzymes)
instructions: Sikhye is a traditional Korean sweet fermented rice drink — essentially a cold rice dessert
The malt barley enzymes convert the rice starch into sugar — this is malting
Mix hot cooked rice with malt barley dissolved in warm water
Keep warm (50-60°C) for 4-8 hours — the enzymes need consistent warm temperature
The rice grains float to the surface as they are digested by the enzymes — a visual signal
Strain, sweeten to taste
Chill
The rice grains that float are removed (traditionally), or kept for texture
Sikhye is slightly sweet, very lightly fermented, refreshing
Served at Korean ancestral rites (jesa), celebrations, and as a digestive after heavy meals
The malt enzyme action is the same biochemistry as brewing beer — but no alcohol develops
Traditional Korean food science in a cup
desserts.description: Korea's ancient sweet rice drink — cooked rice converted by malt barley enzymes into a slightly sweet, cloudy drink over 4-8 hours at controlled temperature. The floating rice grains (a visual signal that the enzymes have done their work) are the traditional marker of success. Sikhye is the Korean digestive drink after heavy meals, and a staple of ancestral rites. Food-science in a cup: malting without fermentation to alcohol.

desserts.name: Yakgwa (Honey Sesame Cookie)
instructions: Yakgwa = 'medicinal confection' — named because honey and ginger were considered medicinal
A Joseon Dynasty royal court confection
Mix flour with honey, sesame oil, ginger juice, rice wine, cinnamon
The sesame oil in the dough creates layers when fried — like a laminated pastry
Press into molds (flower shapes are traditional) or cut into rectangles
Deep fry at low temperature — the slow fry is essential
Low oil temperature (150°C) allows the inside to cook through without burning
After frying: immediately soak in a honey-syrup
The fried cookie absorbs the honey — becomes dense, sweet, honey-saturated
Yakgwa is chewy-dense, intensely honey-flavored, aromatic with ginger and sesame
Traditional for Chuseok (harvest festival) and ancestral rites
One of Korea's oldest confections — recipes unchanged since the Joseon Dynasty
desserts.description: Korea's ancient honey cookie — flour mixed with sesame oil and ginger (both traditionally medicinal, hence 'yakgwa' = medicine confection), fried slowly at low temperature, then soaked in honey syrup. The sesame oil in the dough creates layers like laminated pastry. After honey soaking: dense, chewy, intensely honey-flavored. Unchanged since the Joseon Dynasty. Made for Chuseok and ancestral rites.

drinks.name: Sujeonggwa (Persimmon Punch)
instructions: Boil ginger and cinnamon 30 min
Strain, add sugar
Add dried persimmons, steep
Chill, serve with pine nuts
drinks.description: Sweet cinnamon-ginger punch with dried persimmon.

drinks.name: Makgeolli (Rice Wine)
instructions: Cook rice, cool
Mix with nuruk and water
Ferment 3-7 days
Strain milky liquid

drinks.name: Oksusu Cha (Corn Silk Tea)
ingredients: Dried corn silk (the silky threads from a corn cob — dried in the sun)
instructions: Corn silk tea is a traditional Korean herbal drink — popular throughout the peninsula
The corn silk (the thin threads of the corn cob) is dried and brewed as tea
Corn arrived in Korea from the Americas in the 16th century
The tea: simmer dried corn silk in water 10-15 minutes
Golden-yellow color — light, slightly sweet, subtly corn-flavored
Corn silk has traditional medicinal uses — diuretic, blood pressure
In North Korea, corn (maize) is a significant crop — the silk is utilized too
The zero-waste philosophy: every part of the corn plant has use
Corn silk tea is sold commercially in South Korea and made at home in the North
A gentle, pleasant tea from a commonly discarded ingredient
The subtle sweetness comes from the corn silk itself — no sugar needed
drinks.description: Korea's corn silk tea — the golden threads from dried corn cobs, simmered into a lightly golden, mildly sweet, subtly corn-flavored herbal drink. Traditional medicinal uses include diuretic and blood pressure effects. In North Korea, corn is a significant crop; this tea embodies the Korean zero-waste principle — the silk usually discarded becomes a beverage. Subtly sweet from the silk itself, no added sugar needed.
